scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document is a multicenter Japanese retrospective cohort study (n=515) following COVID-19 survivors for 36 months, explicitly using the CDC definition of long COVID, cluster-classifying patients by long COVID symptom profile, and reporting QOL/economic outcomes; Lyme disease is never mentioned.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a Japanese multicenter study that followed 515 hospitalized COVID-19 patients for three years, asking them repeatedly about symptoms, quality of life, and work productivity. It found that while many symptoms faded over time, fatigue and breathlessness often persisted, and a subset of patients kept experiencing multiple symptoms throughout the three years. Patients whose symptoms were continuous or who had many symptoms reported worse self-rated economic conditions and lower work-productivity scores (presenteeism/absenteeism) than patients whose symptoms resolved. The study measures burden using standardized survey scores (SF-36 quality-of-life score, WHO presenteeism/absenteeism scores) and subjective economic-condition categories, not dollar costs. The authors say that large studies tracking long COVID's long-term socioeconomic impact remain scarce.

contextual_issues: The document mentions, without quantifying, that 'daily life during the pandemic per se' could have affected economic conditions independent of long COVID, since no healthy control group was included.

The document notes a risk of misclassifying reinfection-related symptom recurrence (e.g., fever) as long COVID, because no objective clinical testing (blood tests, imaging) was performed to confirm long COVID versus reinfection.

Vaccination status was associated with lower long COVID prevalence in this cohort (28.0% in vaccinated vs 50.0% in unvaccinated symptomatic patients at 3 months), but this is a symptom-prevalence association, not a modeled economic burden figure.

Comorbidities (asthma, cardiovascular disease, mechanical ventilation use) differed between long COVID and asymptomatic groups, but the document does not translate these into cost or burden estimates.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost data (e.g., healthcare visits, hospitalizations, medication costs) are reported anywhere in the document.
No direct non-medical cost data (travel for care, paid help, assistive devices) are reported.
No caregiving-time or caregiver-burden data are quantified, even though caregiving strain is a plausible consequence of the described disability and reduced work capacity.
No insurance coverage, access-to-care, or care-seeking-frequency (e.g., number of clinic visits, specialist referrals) data are reported.

No dollar-denominated cost-of-illness estimate exists in this document; all economic measures are standardized productivity/QOL survey scores (WHO HPQ presenteeism/absenteeism, SF-36) and self-reported categorical 'economic condition' change, which would require external wage or healthcare-price data to monetize.
No long-term (beyond 36 months) financial consequence data (e.g., job loss, disability benefits, debt) are reported.
comparison_boundaries: Presenteeism, absenteeism (WHO Health and Work Performance Questionnaire) and SF-36 scores are standardized survey instrument scores, not monetized dollar costs, and must not be converted to USD or pooled with cost-of-illness dollar figures from other sources.

spec.title: Long COVID at 36 Months: Work-Performance and Quality-of-Life Gaps (Japanese Hospitalized Cohort)
spec.boundary: This models three standardized-survey-score comparisons (WHO HPQ presenteeism, SF-36 quality of life, self-rated 'economic condition worsened' percentage) reported at 36 months in a single Japanese multicenter cohort of 515 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 during the first three pandemic waves (Jan 2020-Feb 2021). It does not include any dollar-denominated medical cost, caregiving cost, insurance, or long-term financial data, because none are reported anywhere in this document. Results are from one country, one hospitalized cohort, with no uninfected control group, and the authors state they should not be generalized to non-hospitalized patients, later pandemic periods, or other countries.

takeaway.patient: In this study, people who still had long COVID symptoms at the three-year mark reported feeling able to do less of their usual work while at work (a work-performance score of about 59 out of 100, versus about 66 out of 100 for people whose symptoms had resolved) and scored lower on a standard 0-100 quality-of-life questionnaire (about 48 versus 52). People whose symptoms stayed continuous the whole three years were much more likely to say their personal economic situation had gotten worse (about 44%) than people whose symptoms had fully gone away (about 15%). These are group averages from one hospital-based study in Japan, not a prediction for any one person, and the study did not measure medical costs or out-of-pocket spending at all.
takeaway.care: Among hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed 36 months in this cohort, those with persistent long COVID symptoms scored consistently worse than those whose symptoms resolved on standardized work-performance (presenteeism) and quality-of-life (SF-36) measures, and patients whose symptoms remained continuous throughout follow-up were far more likely to report worsened personal economic condition (43.6%) than those who recovered (14.9%). The study also found that patients grouped into a 'multiple persistent symptoms' cluster at 3 months went on to have the worst presenteeism, absenteeism, and SF-36 scores of any symptom cluster at 36 months, suggesting early symptom-cluster assignment could help identify patients needing longer socioeconomic as well as clinical follow-up.
takeaway.policy: This 36-month cohort study reports no dollar-cost figures, but its standardized productivity and quality-of-life scores show a clear gradient: patients with continuous long COVID symptoms were roughly three times more likely to report worsened personal economic condition (43.6%) than patients whose symptoms had resolved (14.9%), and the lowest-functioning symptom cluster (multiple persistent symptoms, n=26) scored worst on quality of life, presenteeism, and absenteeism among five symptom-based clusters. These are standardized survey scores, not monetized costs or utility estimates, and cannot support cost-effectiveness or willingness-to-pay calculations without external wage and healthcare-price data.

patient: If your own COVID symptoms have continued for years rather than resolving, this pattern suggests it may be worth raising work-capacity and quality-of-life concerns with your care team, even if standard tests look normal.

Consider noticing whether your own symptom pattern has been continuous, coming-and-going, or fully resolved over time, since that pattern - more than symptom count alone - was most linked to worse outcomes in this study.
Keep in mind this study did not track medical spending, so it cannot tell you what to expect in out-of-pocket costs; treat that as a separate open question for your own financial planning.
care: Consider whether patients presenting with multiple persistent symptoms at 3 months are being flagged for longer socioeconomic and work-capacity follow-up, not only symptom-focused follow-up, given this cohort's pattern.

Review whether your own follow-up pathway captures symptom trajectory (continuous vs. relapsing vs. resolved) over time rather than just symptom count at a single visit, since trajectory was the strongest signal of productivity and economic impact here.

This finding may be worth checking against your own workflow for connecting long-term clinical follow-up with occupational-health or social-work referral, since the study itself reports no healthcare-utilization or cost data showing what resources these patients actually used.
policy: Consider using the trajectory-based gradient in self-rated economic worsening (continuous vs. relapsing vs. recovered) as a rationale for exploring risk-stratified rather than uniform long COVID support policy, while noting this study itself provides no cost basis for sizing that support.

Flag the absence of any dollar-denominated cost or healthcare-utilization data in this document as a gap when commissioning further long COVID economic-burden research, since standardized survey scores alone cannot feed cost-effectiveness models.

Note the single-country, hospitalized-only, early-pandemic-wave scope of this cohort before applying these figures to policy intended for broader or later populations, per the authors' own stated limitation.

package.documentation:
This simulator reproduces three 36-month outcome comparisons from a Japanese multicenter cohort study of 515 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 during the first three pandemic waves (Jan 2020-Feb 2021), all measured with standardized survey instruments rather than dollar costs: the WHO Health and Work Performance Questionnaire (HPQ) absolute presenteeism score (0-100; higher = closer to expected work performance while present), the SF-36 quality-of-life score (0-100), and a self-reported 'economic condition worsened' percentage. The presenteeism and SF-36 comparisons are long-COVID-group vs. asymptomatic-group at 36 months (Table 1, p.3); the economic-worsening comparison is continuous-symptom vs. fully-recovered trajectory groups at 36 months (p.7, Fig. 5a description). No medical costs, caregiving costs, insurance data, or other dollar-denominated figures appear anywhere in the source document, so this tool cannot and does not estimate a monetary cost of long COVID.

Input ranges for the three paired comparisons were each narrowed from the full plausible scale so that slider exploration cannot generate a result reversing the study's own reported direction (long COVID / continuous-symptom groups scoring worse); these narrower bounds are an assumed, illustrative exploration choice, not values reported in the document. All default values are the study's own reported means or percentages. The data_period field for each input has been normalized to '2023', an assumed value representing the approximate publication/reporting period of the 36-month follow-up data, since the document does not state a specific calendar data_period format for these survey measurements; this is a labeling correction only and does not change any reported score or percentage.

Sex and gender: the same research group's earlier 12-month analysis found higher long COVID risk in women (odds ratio 2.54, 95% CI 1.43-4.53); by 36 months the proportion with vs. without long COVID no longer differed significantly by sex (p=0.18), leading the authors to state that sex's influence appeared to lessen by three years. None of the economic/productivity outcomes modeled here (presenteeism, SF-36, economic-condition percentages) have themselves been reported broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity in this document, even though sex and age were collected for the cohort; federal survey instruments such as MEPS, NHIS, and BRFSS generally do support this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this study did not perform it, so the pooled figures here should not be assumed to apply equally across subgroups.

Limitations: this is a single-country, single-cohort study of hospitalized patients from the first three pandemic waves; the authors state results should not be generalized to non-hospitalized patients, later variants or periods, or other countries. No uninfected control group was included, so some reported economic worsening could reflect general pandemic conditions rather than long COVID specifically, per the authors' own stated caveat. The symptom-cluster subgroups referenced in the underlying study are uneven in size (n=26 to n=307) and are not of equal statistical precision.

spec.title: Long COVID at 36 Months: Work-Performance and Quality-of-Life Gaps (Japanese Hospitalized Cohort)
spec.boundary: This models three standardized-survey-score comparisons (WHO HPQ presenteeism, SF-36 quality of life, self-rated 'economic condition worsened' percentage) reported at 36 months in a single Japanese multicenter cohort of 515 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 during the first three pandemic waves (Jan 2020-Feb 2021). It does not include any dollar-denominated medical cost, caregiving cost, insurance, or long-term financial data, because none are reported anywhere in this document. Results are from one country, one hospitalized cohort, with no uninfected control group, and the authors state they should not be generalized to non-hospitalized patients, later pandemic periods, or other countries.

takeaway.patient: In this study, people who still had long COVID symptoms at the three-year mark reported feeling able to do less of their usual work while at work (a work-performance score of about 59 out of 100, versus about 66 out of 100 for people whose symptoms had resolved) and scored lower on a standard 0-100 quality-of-life questionnaire (about 48 versus 52). People whose symptoms stayed continuous the whole three years were much more likely to say their personal economic situation had gotten worse (about 44%) than people whose symptoms had fully gone away (about 15%). These are group averages from one hospital-based study in Japan, not a prediction for any one person, and the study did not measure medical costs or out-of-pocket spending at all.
takeaway.care: Among hospitalized COVID-19 patients followed 36 months in this cohort, those with persistent long COVID symptoms scored consistently worse than those whose symptoms resolved on standardized work-performance (presenteeism) and quality-of-life (SF-36) measures, and patients whose symptoms remained continuous throughout follow-up were far more likely to report worsened personal economic condition (43.6%) than those who recovered (14.9%). The study also found that patients grouped into a 'multiple persistent symptoms' cluster at 3 months went on to have the worst presenteeism, absenteeism, and SF-36 scores of any symptom cluster at 36 months, suggesting early symptom-cluster assignment could help identify patients needing longer socioeconomic as well as clinical follow-up.
takeaway.policy: This 36-month cohort study reports no dollar-cost figures, but its standardized productivity and quality-of-life scores show a clear gradient: patients with continuous long COVID symptoms were roughly three times more likely to report worsened personal economic condition (43.6%) than patients whose symptoms had resolved (14.9%), and the lowest-functioning symptom cluster (multiple persistent symptoms, n=26) scored worst on quality of life, presenteeism, and absenteeism among five symptom-based clusters. These are standardized survey scores, not monetized costs or utility estimates, and cannot support cost-effectiveness or willingness-to-pay calculations without external wage and healthcare-price data.

patient: If your own COVID symptoms have continued for years rather than resolving, this pattern suggests it may be worth raising work-capacity and quality-of-life concerns with your care team, even if standard tests look normal.

Consider noticing whether your own symptom pattern has been continuous, coming-and-going, or fully resolved over time, since that pattern - more than symptom count alone - was most linked to worse outcomes in this study.
Keep in mind this study did not track medical spending, so it cannot tell you what to expect in out-of-pocket costs; treat that as a separate open question for your own financial planning.
care: Consider whether patients presenting with multiple persistent symptoms at 3 months are being flagged for longer socioeconomic and work-capacity follow-up, not only symptom-focused follow-up, given this cohort's pattern.

Review whether your own follow-up pathway captures symptom trajectory (continuous vs. relapsing vs. resolved) over time rather than just symptom count at a single visit, since trajectory was the strongest signal of productivity and economic impact here.

This finding may be worth checking against your own workflow for connecting long-term clinical follow-up with occupational-health or social-work referral, since the study itself reports no healthcare-utilization or cost data showing what resources these patients actually used.
policy: Consider using the trajectory-based gradient in self-rated economic worsening (continuous vs. relapsing vs. recovered) as a rationale for exploring risk-stratified rather than uniform long COVID support policy, while noting this study itself provides no cost basis for sizing that support.

Flag the absence of any dollar-denominated cost or healthcare-utilization data in this document as a gap when commissioning further long COVID economic-burden research, since standardized survey scores alone cannot feed cost-effectiveness models.

Note the single-country, hospitalized-only, early-pandemic-wave scope of this cohort before applying these figures to policy intended for broader or later populations, per the authors' own stated limitation.
